The widths of the confidence intervals are driven by increasing uncertainty as the time horizon extends. For the 1-week horizon, external influences or variability have a greater chance to impact the outcome, so the interval naturally widens from 29.43 to 31.13. At one month, the uncertainty grows further, covering the range from 28.75 to 32.25, as more complex or unpredictable factors—such as market shifts, environmental variability, or other systemic influences—play a role. This widening reflects that projecting farther into the future inherently involves compounding uncertainties.

Specific risks or unexpected events could push the outcomes beyond the stated intervals. For example, a sudden and highly impactful event—like an economic shock, a major policy change, or an unforeseen crisis—could disrupt the stability assumed in this forecast. Additionally, any extreme behavioral or structural changes in the system being modeled (e.g., sudden spikes in volatility or shifts due to external dependencies) would also pose a challenge. These are harder to predict and quantify but should always remain a consideration when interpreting probabilistic forecasts.
